title: What is BFS (Breadth First Search) — visit all neighbors first before going deeper (use a queue); like exploring a maze level by level.

s1_definition.profdef: Breadth-first search is a graph and tree traversal that explores all vertices at the current distance from the start before moving to vertices one step farther away. It uses a queue to process vertices in the order they are discovered and a visited set to avoid revisiting. Because it expands outward level by level, BFS finds the shortest path in terms of number of edges in an unweighted graph, running in time proportional to vertices plus edges.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the fraud team at the National Bank of India starting from Rajesh's account and asking who received money directly from him. Those are the first ring. Then they ask who those people sent money to next — the second ring. They finish checking everyone one hop away before looking at anyone two hops away. This ripple-outward search, like dropping a stone in a pond and watching the circles spread, is breadth-first search.
s1_definition.oneliner: BFS explores a graph ring by ring using a queue, so it finds the fewest-hops path first.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Breadth-first search is a graph and tree traversal that explores all vertices at the current distance from the start before moving to vertices one step farther away. It uses a queue to process vertices in the order they are discovered and a visited set to avoid revisiting. Because it expands outward level by level, BFS finds the shortest path in terms of number of edges in an unweighted graph, running in time proportional to vertices plus edges.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the fraud team at the National Bank of India starting from Rajesh's account and asking who received money directly from him. Those are the first ring. Then they ask who those people sent money to next — the second ring. They finish checking everyone one hop away before looking at anyone two hops away. This ripple-outward search, like dropping a stone in a pond and watching the circles spread, is breadth-first search.

**One line to remember:** BFS explores a graph ring by ring using a queue, so it finds the fewest-hops path first.

sections.s2_technical:
BFS relies on two structures: a queue holding the vertices to visit next, and a visited set preventing cycles from causing infinite loops. The algorithm starts by adding the source to the queue and marking it visited.

The main loop dequeues a vertex, processes it, and enqueues each of its unvisited neighbours while marking them visited. For example `String current = queue.poll();` takes the next vertex, then `for (String neighbour : graph.neighbours(current)) { if (visited.add(neighbour)) queue.offer(neighbour); }` enqueues each new neighbour. Using the boolean return of `visited.add` cleverly both checks and marks in one step, because add returns false if the element was already present.

The queue is essential because it enforces the level-by-level order. Everything one hop away is enqueued before anything two hops away is reached, so vertices come out of the queue in increasing distance from the source. This is precisely why BFS yields shortest paths in unweighted graphs: the first time you reach a vertex, you have reached it by the fewest possible edges. To recover the actual path you store a parent pointer for each vertex as you discover it.

A senior-level point is complexity and memory. BFS visits each vertex and edge once, so it is linear in vertices plus edges. Its memory can be large because the queue may hold an entire level, which for a wide graph is substantial. BFS is the right choice for shortest path in unweighted graphs, for finding all nodes within k hops, and for level-order processing. When edges have weights you need Dijkstra instead, and when you only need to know if a path exists and memory is tight, depth-first search may be preferable.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India fraud team suspects a mule network and wants to know, starting from Rajesh's account, every account reachable through chains of transfers and how many hops away each one is. Finding reachable accounts in increasing distance order is exactly what breadth-first search does, rippling outward one hop at a time.

Problem 2 — The team specifically cares about the shortest chain of transfers connecting Rajesh to a suspicious account, because the fewer the hops the stronger the link. Since each transfer counts as one hop with no weight, BFS gives the minimum-hop path directly, the first time it reaches the target.

In our mini-project we build a `MoneyFlowBFS` that performs BFS over a transfer graph, printing each account with its hop distance from the start. The demo builds a small transfer network, runs BFS from Rajesh's account, and logs the reach and distances.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: a transfer graph where SAV2001 sends to CUR3001 and SAV4002, both of which send to SAV5003, which sends to CUR6004. We start BFS from SAV2001.

Step 1: We enqueue SAV2001, mark it visited, and set its distance to zero. The queue holds SAV2001.

Step 2: We dequeue SAV2001 and process it at distance zero. Its neighbours CUR3001 and SAV4002 are new, so we mark them visited, set their distance to one, and enqueue both.

Step 3: We dequeue CUR3001 at distance one. Its neighbour SAV5003 is new, so we mark it, set its distance to two, and enqueue it.

Step 4: We dequeue SAV4002 at distance one. Its neighbour SAV5003 is already visited, so we skip it. This is the visited set preventing duplicate work.

Step 5: We dequeue SAV5003 at distance two. Its neighbour CUR6004 is new, so we mark it, set its distance to three, and enqueue it.

Step 6: We dequeue CUR6004 at distance three. It has no neighbours. The queue is now empty, so BFS ends having reached five accounts, each labelled with its minimum hop distance from Rajesh.

```
[2026-10-26 20:25:03] INFO    Reached SAV2001 at 0 hop(s)
[2026-10-26 20:25:03] INFO    Reached CUR3001 at 1 hop(s)
[2026-10-26 20:25:03] INFO    Reached SAV4002 at 1 hop(s)
[2026-10-26 20:25:03] INFO    Reached SAV5003 at 2 hop(s)
[2026-10-26 20:25:03] INFO    Reached CUR6004 at 3 hop(s)
[2026-10-26 20:25:03] INFO    BFS complete. Reachable accounts: 5
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Start SAV2001 (ring 0)
    │ enqueue neighbours
    ▼
  Ring 1: CUR3001, SAV4002        distance 1
    │
    ▼
  Ring 2: SAV5003                 distance 2 (reached via CUR3001;
    │                              SAV4002→SAV5003 skipped, already visited)
    ▼
  Ring 3: CUR6004                 distance 3

  Queue order: [SAV2001] → [CUR3001,SAV4002] → [SAV5003] → [CUR6004] → []
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Breadth-first search is a traversal that explores a graph ring by ring, visiting every vertex at the current distance from the start before moving to vertices one step farther away. It uses a queue to process vertices in discovery order and a visited set to avoid revisiting, which also prevents cycles from causing an infinite loop. Because it expands outward evenly, the first time BFS reaches any vertex it has reached it by the fewest possible edges, so BFS gives the shortest path in an unweighted graph.

The mechanics are simple and I always describe them precisely. I start by enqueuing the source and marking it visited. Then I loop: dequeue a vertex, process it, and for each neighbour that has not been visited, mark it and enqueue it. A neat trick is using the boolean return of the visited set's add method, which both checks and marks in one step because add returns false if the element was already there. The queue is what enforces the level order, since everything one hop away is enqueued before anything two hops away is reached.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used BFS in fraud analysis. Starting from a suspect account like Rajesh's, the fraud team wants every account reachable through chains of transfers and how many hops away each one is, because a wide reach in few hops suggests a mule network. Since each transfer is a single unweighted hop, BFS gives both the reachable set and the minimum-hop distance to each account in one pass, and by storing a parent pointer I can reconstruct the actual shortest chain.

The senior-level points I add are about complexity and tool selection. BFS is linear in vertices plus edges, but its memory can be heavy because the queue may hold an entire level at once, which matters for very wide graphs. BFS is the right tool for shortest paths in unweighted graphs and for finding everything within k hops, but the moment edges carry weights like fees I switch to Dijkstra, and if I only need to know whether a path exists and memory is tight, depth-first search is often the leaner choice.
